definition: To move someone or something to a lower, less important, or less noticeable place.
example: A single harsh review can relegate a promising young restaurant to obscurity.
nuance: Demote usually means lowering an official rank, while relegate more broadly pushes something aside, often out of sight or attention.
prompt: A museum curator is rearranging the galleries before a new exhibit opens.
options: The curator chose to relegate the faded tapestries to a dim back hallway.
To celebrate its arrival, the curator will relegate the prized new sculpture to the center of the main hall.
During the tour, the curator tried to relegate the guests with funny stories about the artists.
Staff relegate the gallery temperature each morning to protect the canvases.
reasons: Moving worn pieces out of the spotlight to a minor spot is exactly the right use.
Giving a piece the place of honor raises its status; it does not push it down.
Entertaining people with stories is regaling them, a look-alike word.
Controlling temperature is regulating it; nothing is being lowered in importance.

practice.prompt: A school newspaper editor is planning the layout of this week's issue.
options: At the staff meeting, the editor tried to relegate the new writers with tales of her first big interview.
The editor asked a student to relegate her message to the print shop by phone before noon.
Short on space, the editor had to relegate the chess club results to a small box on page eight.
Thrilled by the scoop, the editor decided to relegate the story to the top of the front page.
reasons: Amusing listeners with tales is regaling, not pushing anyone into a minor role.
Passing a message along is relaying it; the word does not mean deliver.
Shrinking a story and burying it deep in the paper gives it a lesser position.
The front page is the most prominent spot, so this reverses the meaning.
